terms.gloss: consist of, be made up of
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, intransitive, with ex and the ablative
evidence: Cic. N.D. 1.98: homō ex animō cōnstat et corpore (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In Cicero always with ex (Lewis & Short). The verb has other common senses: to stand firm, to be consistent (sibi cōnstāre), to cost (with the genitive or ablative of price), and, impersonally, cōnstat, “it is agreed, everyone knows”.

phrases.latin: homō ex animō cōnstat et corpore
phrases.english: a human being consists of soul and body
the plain (sauce) consists of sweet olive oil

phrases.latin: Ex quibus rēbus cōnstat haec placenta?
phrases.english: What is this cake made of?

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 245, 296, checked against the searchable text of the book (11 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.
